title: How many uniforms to exceed one?
objectives: Find the expected number of uniform draws until their sum exceeds one.

screens.title: Two draws
screens.prose: Draw uniforms on $[0, 1]$ and add them until the sum passes 1. Let $N$ be the number of draws. Drag the point $(u_1, u_2)$: below the line, two draws are not yet enough.

derive.caption: $u_1 + u_2$ = {{fixed(P.x + P.y, 2)}}: {{P.x + P.y <= 1 ? "not past 1, so draw again" : "past 1 after two draws"}}.

screens.question: What is the chance two uniforms sum to at most 1? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: The square has area 1, so area is chance.
The event is the shaded triangle below the line.

feedback.correct: The triangle under $u_1 + u_2 = 1$ has area $\tfrac12$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the area of the shaded triangle.

byKey.quarter: You multiplied two halves. The two draws do not each need to be under a half.

explain.text: The event $u_1 + u_2 \le 1$ is the triangle under the line, area $\tfrac12$. So $P(N > 2) = \tfrac12$. Half the time two draws are not enough.

screens.title: Three draws
screens.prose: Three draws sum to at most 1 when the first two fit under $1 - u_3$. Slide the third draw: the triangle shrinks to area $(1 - u_3)^2/2$.

derive.caption: Third draw {{fixed(w, 2)}}: the first two must sum to at most {{fixed(1 - w, 2)}}, an area of {{fixed(pow(1 - w, 2) / 2, 3)}}.

screens.question: What is $P(U_1 + U_2 + U_3 \le 1)$? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Average the shaded area over $u_3$ uniform on $[0, 1]$.

feedback.correct: $\int_0^1 \tfrac{(1 - w)^2}{2}\,dw = \tfrac16$: the corner of the cube.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the triangle's area as the third draw slides.

byKey.third: You guessed $\tfrac1n$. The corner shrinks faster than that.
byKey.halves: You multiplied three halves. The draws need not each be under a half.

explain.text: The slices are triangles of area $(1 - w)^2/2$. Stacked up, they form the corner $u_1 + u_2 + u_3 \le 1$ of the cube. Its volume is $\tfrac16$.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose: So $N > n$ exactly when the first $n$ draws sum to at most 1. That event is the corner of an $n$-dimensional cube.
screens.question: What is $P(N > 4)$? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Look at how each row follows from the last.
Each new draw divides by the new $n$: $1, \tfrac12, \tfrac16$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The pattern is $\tfrac1{n!}$.

byKey.quarter: You took $\tfrac1n$. The chances shrink like $\tfrac1{n!}$.
byKey.sixteenth: You took $(\tfrac12)^4$. The corner is smaller than that.

explain.text: The corner of the $n$-cube has volume $\tfrac1{n!}$, so $P(N > 4) = \tfrac1{24}$. Each slice argument divides by one more $n$.

screens.title: The expected count
screens.prose: For a count, $E[N] = \sum_{n \ge 0} P(N > n)$. Here that is $1 + 1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac16 + \tfrac1{24} + \dots$ The engine's own seeded run shows the running average settling.
screens.question: What is $E[N]$? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: It is the series for $e^x$ at $x = 1$.

byKey.two: That is the trap on the next screen. Two draws pass 1 only half the time.
byKey.three: Three is common, but $N = 2$ half the time pulls the average below 3.
byKey.short: You stopped the series at $\tfrac16$. The tail adds about 0.05 more.

explain.text: The tail chances are $\tfrac1{n!}$, and they add to $e$. Over all 4,000 trials the running average settles on the line at $e$. Its wobble shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$.

screens.title: Two, surely?
screens.prose: An interviewer asks how many uniforms it takes, on average, for the sum to pass 1. A candidate says at once: "the average uniform is a half, so two."
screens.question: What is the expected number of draws?

options.why: You reasoned from the average draw. Two draws pass 1 only half the time, and many runs need three or more.
Three is common, but half of all runs stop at two.
The tail chances $\tfrac1{n!}$ shrink fast, so the sum is finite.

hints.text: $N$ is at least 2, and more than 2 half the time.

feedback.correct: $e \approx 2.72$: $N$ is at least 2 and often more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $N$ is never below 2, and often above it.

byKey.two: You divided 1 by the mean draw $\tfrac12$. That treats the sum as landing on 1 exactly, but it passes 1.

explain.text: $N \ge 2$ always, and $N > 2$ half the time, so $E[N] > 2$. The reasoning "1 divided by a half" ignores the overshoot past 1. The answer is $e$.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose:
Write $P(N > n)$ as a volume, then add the tails:

$$E[N] = \sum_{n \ge 0} P(N > n), \qquad P(U_1 + \dots + U_n \le t) = \frac{t^n}{n!} \text{ for } t \le 1.$$
screens.question: What is the expected number of uniforms to pass $\tfrac12$? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The corner of side $t$ has volume $t^n/n!$.

byKey.e: That is for $t = 1$. A lower level needs fewer draws.
byKey.one: One draw passes $\tfrac12$ only half the time.
byKey.lin: You halved $e$. The answer is $e^t$, not $t \cdot e$.

explain.text: The corner shrinks to $t^n/n!$, so $E[N] = e^t$. At $t = \tfrac12$ that is 1.6487. The formula holds for $t \le 1$ only.

screens.title: Why $e$
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: $N > n$ exactly when the first $n$ uniforms sum to at most 1.
That event is the corner $u_1 + \dots + u_n \le 1$ of the unit cube, of volume $\tfrac1{n!}$.
That is the series for $e^1$: $E[N] = e \approx 2.7183$.

hints.text: Then its volume, then the tail-sum formula.

feedback.correct: The event, its volume, the tail sum, then the series.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn $N > n$ into a volume first.

byKey.d1: The stopped sum averages $E[N]/2$, but it passes 1. So it is not equal to 1.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the one dividing by $\tfrac12$ belongs.

explain.text: Each line rests on the one before: the event, its volume, then the tail sum. The tail sum turns volumes into $e$. The line dividing by $\tfrac12$ forgets the overshoot.

screens.question: Write the simulation.

widget.solution:
import random


def exceed_one_sim(trials, seed):
    """Average number of uniforms needed for the sum to pass 1."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    total = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        s, n = 0.0, 0
        while s <= 1:
            s += rng.random()
            n += 1
        total += n
    return total / trials
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Tests 1 to 3 accept an average within three standard errors of $e$. The standard deviation of $N$ is about 0.875. Test 4 checks one trial needs two draws or more. Test 5 runs one seed twice, and test 6 wants a float.

hints.text: Add each trial's count to a total.

feedback.correct: The simulated average sits within the noise of $e$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: The average is far from 2.718. Check that each trial starts a fresh sum at 0 and stops once it passes 1.
byKey.test-4: One trial always needs at least two draws. Count the draw that passes 1.

explain.text: With seed 1 and 20,000 trials the model solution gives 2.7158. The standard error is $0.875/\sqrt{20000} \approx 0.006$. Each extra digit costs a hundred times the trials.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three puzzles at about 3 minutes each, 9 in all; keep your own time. $N$ counts uniforms until the sum passes 1. Four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

explain.text: Differences of tails give $P(N = 2) = \tfrac12$ and $P(N = 3) = \tfrac13$. Summing $(2n + 1)/n!$ gives $E[N^2] = 3e$. So $\text{Var}(N) = 3e - e^2 \approx 0.7658$.

screens.title: Follow-up: where does it stop?
screens.prose: You gave $e$. The interviewer asks for the expected sum at the moment it first passes 1, $E[S_N]$. Wald's identity says $E[S_N] = E[N] \, E[U]$ when $N$ is a stopping time with a finite mean, as here: $E[N] = e$.
screens.question: What is $E[S_N]$? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: $N$ is a stopping time with finite mean: it depends only on draws so far, and $E[N] = e$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $E[N]$ by the mean draw.

byKey.one: The sum stops past 1, never at it. So the answer is above 1.
byKey.half: You assumed the overshoot averages a half. Wald's identity gives it exactly.

explain.text: Whether we stop at draw $n$ depends only on the first $n$ draws, and $E[N] = e$ is finite, so Wald applies. $E[S_N] = e \times \tfrac12 \approx 1.3591$. The average overshoot is 0.3591.

screens.title: Filling a parent order
screens.prose: A broker works a 10,000-share parent order in child fills. Each fill is uniform on 0 to 12,500 shares, independent of the others.
screens.question: What is the expected number of fills to complete the order? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Measure in units of the largest fill, 12,500 shares.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rescale so fills are uniform on $[0, 1]$, then use $e^t$.

byKey.e: You took $t = 1$. The order is only 0.8 of the largest fill.
byKey.mean: You divided 10,000 by the mean fill of 6,250. That ignores the last fill's overshoot.

explain.text: In units of 12,500 shares the order is $t = 0.8$. The corner argument gives $e^{0.8} \approx 2.23$ fills. Dividing by the mean fill gives 1.6, the same mistake as the trap.
